header: Muhammad Waseem and another Vs The State and another
Order with the signature of the Judge and that of parties or counsel where
16.10.2026 Mr. Muhammad Amir Khan Bhutta, Advocate, for the
Mr. Adnan Latif Sheikh, Deputy Prosecutor General, with
Ch. Khalid Mehmood Arian, Advocate, for the Complainant.
body: Tariq Saleem Sheikh, J. – Through this application under section 497 Cr.P.C., Petitioners Muhammad Waseem and Naveed seek post-arrest bail in case FIR No.41/2026 dated 18.01.2026, registered at Police Station Chab Kalan, District Khanewal, under section 375-A PPC. The prosecution alleges that the Petitioners, along with their coaccused, sexually assaulted M.R., the grandson of Respondent No.2, who was approximately eight years old at the relevant time.

2. According to their respective Forms-B, Muhammad Waseem was born on 24.06.2010 and Naveed on 17.05.2010. Both were, therefore, below sixteen years of age at the time of the alleged occurrence. They were arrested on 20.01.2026. Their applications for post-arrest bail were initially dismissed on merits by the Additional Sessions Judge, Mian Channu, on 07.03.2026. They subsequently approached this Court through Crl. Misc. No. 2890-B/2026, which was dismissed as withdrawn on 18.05.2026. Their next application, moved on the statutory ground of delay in conclusion of trial, was withdrawn before the Additional Sessions Judge on 17.07.2026. They thereafter filed another application on the same ground, which the Additional Crl. Misc. No.7524-B/2026 2 Sessions Judge dismissed on 15.09.2026, holding that the delay was attributable to the defence. Hence, the present application.

3. Mr. Muhammad Amir Khan Bhutta, Advocate, contends that the Petitioners have been in continuous detention for more than six months without conclusion of their trial and are entitled to bail under section 6(5) of the Juvenile Justice System Act, 2018 (JJSA). He submits that the prosecution failed to produce witnesses on several dates, while on other occasions the Petitioners were not produced from custody. Conversely, the Deputy Prosecutor General and counsel for Respondent No. 2 submit that the Petitioners face a grave accusation involving the sexual assault of a child and that the medical evidence supports the prosecution case. They further contend that defence counsel repeatedly sought adjournments despite the attendance of prosecution witnesses and delayed their cross-examination. According to them, the Petitioners cannot claim statutory bail when their own counsel contributed to the failure to conclude the trial within the prescribed period.

4. Section 375-A PPC is punishable with death, imprisonment for the remainder of natural life or imprisonment for life and fine. Having regard to the nature of the accusation and the prescribed punishment, it falls within the definition of a heinous offence under section 2(g) of the JJSA. Section 6(5) provides:

(5) Where the Juvenile Court is of the opinion that the delay in the trial of a juvenile has not been occasioned by an act or omission of such juvenile or any other person acting on his behalf or in exercise of any right or privilege under any law for the time being in force, such juvenile shall be released on bail if he has been detained for a continuous period exceeding six months and whose trial has not been completed.

5. In Mehran v. Ubaid Ullah and others (PLD 2024 SC 843), a three-member Bench of the Supreme Court held that section 6(5) of the JJSA provides a separate ground for bail to a juvenile detained for a heinous offence, irrespective of his age, once the statutory conditions are satisfied. The period of detention runs from the Crl. Misc. No.7524-B/2026 3 date of arrest. The Court further held that the heinous nature of the offence does not justify withholding bail under subsection (5). The gravity of the accusation against the Petitioners, therefore, cannot determine their entitlement on the statutory ground.

6. Section 6(5) of the JJSA substantially reproduces the provisions relating to responsibility for delay contained in section 10(7) of the Juvenile Justice System Ordinance, 2000, and the third proviso to section 497(1) Cr.P.C. as it stood when the Supreme Court decided Zahid Hussain Shah v. The State (PLD 1995 SC 49). Although these provisions prescribed different periods of detention, the principles on attribution of delay remain relevant. In Zahid Hussain Shah, the Supreme Court held that the right to bail upon fulfilment of the statutory conditions was not subject to the Court’s ordinary discretion. Examining the trial record, the Court found that the accused had obtained only two adjournments for specific procedural purposes, and that the case had otherwise been adjourned “for reasons not attributable to the appellant.” It accordingly held that he could not be denied bail on the statutory ground.

7. In Shakeel Shah v. The State and others (2022 SCMR 1), again interpreting the third proviso to section 497(1) Cr.P.C., the Supreme Court explained that adjournments sought by defence counsel do not necessarily disentitle an accused to bail on the statutory ground. Such adjournments may justify refusal of bail where they are sought without sufficient cause on crucial hearing dates fixed for the examination or cross-examination of prosecution witnesses, or are repetitive and reflect a design or pattern consciously to delay the conclusion of the trial. The Court further held that merely counting the adjournments obtained by the defence is insufficient to deny statutory bail. The prosecution must show, on the basis of the record, a concerted effort by the accused or his counsel to delay the conclusion of the trial. In Rohan Ahmad v. The State and others (PLD 2024 SC 492), a three-member Bench reiterated these principles and emphasised Crl. Misc. No.7524-B/2026 4 that the prosecution must demonstrate a concerted and consistent effort to prolong the trial through unnecessary adjournments or irrelevant applications. In Nadeem Samson v. The State and others (PLD 2022 SC 112), the Supreme Court clarified that delay caused by the accused after expiry of the prescribed period is irrelevant for determining his entitlement to statutory bail. Although these judgments interpreted the third proviso to section 497(1) Cr.P.C., the principles relating to responsibility for delay are equally relevant to section 6(5) of the JJSA. The Court must, therefore, examine whether the conduct of the juvenile or a person acting on his behalf occasioned delay before expiry of that period.

8. The Petitioners were arrested on 20.01.2026 and completed six months of detention on 20.07.2026. The challan was submitted on 14.05.2026, and the trial court framed the charge on 21.05.2026. On 08.06.2026, the Presiding Officer was on casual leave and no prosecution witness appeared. On 14.07.2026, two prosecution witnesses attended, but defence counsel sought an adjournment because he was engaged in another case. On 17.07.2026, the trial court recorded the examination-in-chief of the Complainant and M.R., but deferred their cross-examination at defence counsel’s request. The order of that date does not record the reason for the request. According to the trial court’s subsequent report dated 06.10.2026, counsel had not prepared his case.

9. The Additional Sessions Judge dismissed the Petitioners’ previous bail application on 15.09.2026, but incorrectly recorded that the Complainant and M.R. were cross-examined on 17.09.2026. The trial court’s record shows that their cross-examination was completed on 07.09.2026. His further observation that no fresh ground had arisen was also incorrect, since the earlier application had been withdrawn on 17.07.2026, before the Petitioners completed six months of detention. These errors require this Court to examine the Petitioners’ claim independently in light of the record.

Crl. Misc. No.7524-B/2026 5 10. The two adjournments obtained by defence counsel on 14.07.2026 and 17.07.2026 were unjustified and interrupted prosecution evidence on crucial hearing dates. Their significance must, however, be considered in the context of the entire proceedings. The available order sheets disclose no other request for adjournment or miscellaneous application by the defence before 20.07.2026. The trial had made limited progress, and the medical officer, duty officer, moharrar and investigating officer remained unexamined when the statutory period expired. In these circumstances, the prosecution has not shown a concerted and consistent effort by the Petitioners or their counsel to prolong the trial, as contemplated in Shakeel Shah and Rohan Ahmad. The adjournments obtained by the defence after 20.07.2026 are not relevant to the Petitioners’ entitlement, as held in Nadeem Samson. I am, therefore, satisfied that the conditions of section 6(5) of the JJSA have been fulfilled.

11. In view of the above, this application is allowed. The Petitioners are admitted to post-arrest bail, subject to each furnishing a bail bond in the sum of Rs. 200,000/- with one surety in the like amount to the satisfaction of the trial court. The observations made herein are confined to the determination of bail on the statutory ground and shall not influence the trial court’s assessment of the evidence.

12. Before parting with this order, I consider it necessary to refer to the statutory requirements for expeditious disposal of the trial. Section 16(1) of the Anti-Rape (Investigation and Trial) Act, 2021 (the “Anti-Rape Act”) requires the Special Court to decide a case involving a scheduled offence, including section 375-A PPC, expeditiously, preferably within four months of taking cognizance. Subsection (2) restricts adjournments during the trial to two, one of which must be subject to payment of costs by the person seeking it. Where defence counsel fails to appear after two consecutive adjournments, the Court may appoint another counsel having at least seven years’ standing in criminal matters from the panel maintained by the Special Committee. Crl. Misc. No.7524-B/2026 6 Section 4(8) of the JJSA requires the Juvenile Court to decide a case within six months of taking cognizance. If the case is not decided within that period, subsection (9) requires the Court to seek an extension from the High Court and explain the reasons for the delay. If no extension is sought, the complainant or the juvenile may apply to the High Court. These provisions can be applied together. The four-month period under the Anti-Rape Act is expressed as a preference, while the JJSA prescribes a six-month period and provides for extension. Both address the timely disposal of trials, whereas section 6(5) of the JJSA provides for bail on account of prolonged detention, subject to its statutory conditions.

13. In exercise of the powers conferred by section 19 of the Anti-Rape Act, the Ministry of Law and Justice made the Anti-Rape (Trial Procedure) Rules, 2022, notified through S.R.O. 186(I)/2023 (the Procedure Rules). Rule 3 requires the Special Court, after framing the charge, to hold a scheduling hearing, prepare a trial schedule specifying the dates for each stage of the proceedings and issue a trial scheduling certificate. The certificate must be placed on the case file and copies supplied to the persons specified in the Rule. Under Rule 3(6), the special prosecutor must confirm the availability of witnesses, evidence and expert reports three days before commencement of the trial. Rule 4 provides for determining the manner in which the trial will proceed, including arrangements for a child victim or vulnerable witness. Rule 5 regulates the frequency of hearings and adjournments, while Rule 7(8) requires the Court, as far as possible, to record the victim’s examination-in-chief, cross-examination and re-examination on the same day.

14. In the present case, the available order sheets do not disclose that the trial court held a scheduling hearing or issued a trial scheduling certificate after framing the charge on 21.05.2026. The subsequent proceedings also suffered interruptions, including nonproduction of the Petitioners from custody and adjournments of Crl. Misc. No.7524-B/2026 7 prosecution evidence. The trial court shall take necessary steps to secure the attendance of witnesses, regulate adjournments in accordance with the Anti-Rape Act and the Procedure Rules, and conclude the trial expeditiously.

15. All Special Courts constituted or designated under the Anti-Rape Act shall comply with the Procedure Rules, particularly those relating to trial scheduling, recording of evidence, adjournments and safeguards for child victims. They shall also observe the timeframe prescribed by section 16 of the Act. The Senior Additional Registrar of this Bench shall circulate a copy of this order to all District and Sessions Judges in Punjab for communication to the Special Courts concerned and compliance.
